personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Ron is loyal, brave, and emotionally reactive, with a characteristic humor that blends self-deprecation, sarcasm, and well-timed comic deflection. He speaks in direct, often blunt sentences, is quick to anger, quick to laugh, and his voice has a distinctive working-class warmth. He is not primarily comic relief — he is a strategist, an initiator, someone whose jealousy and insecurity coexist with genuine courage and moral clarity. His most important speech pattern is honest emotional candor: he says what he thinks, sometimes regrettably, and his emotional outbursts are followed by genuine remorse. His flaws — jealousy, impulsiveness when wearing the Horcrux, a tendency to feel overshadowed — are inseparable from his personality. In the tent deterioration sequence (Scenes 1016–1115), Ron's cruelty under the Horcrux's influence is specifically shaped: he voices fears about being least loved, about his family dying, about Hermione choosing Harry. These are real wounds, not just Horcrux distortions.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve the core personality traits with reasonable fidelity. Ron's humor is present throughout: 'That's unfortunate' after Bogrod's death (Film Scene 47), 'I'll kill you, Harry' during the Room of Requirement rescue (Film Scene 62), the 'Can't believe I just said that' after praising Malfoy (Film Scene 67), the running joke about being Ginny's forgotten brother (Film Scene 55). His bluntness is preserved in 'Piss off' to Percy at the Ministry (Film Scene 18), his protective instincts in 'Don't touch her!' (Film Scene 34). The departure and Horcrux argument scene (Film Scene 24) preserves his emotional breakdown, including the 'Your parents are dead, you have no family' line. The Deluminator return scene (Film Scenes 25–27) preserves his vulnerability and self-awareness about having run out. His use of the Deluminator, his casting of Imperio at the Ministry (Film Scene 44), and his Parseltongue entry into the Chamber (Film Scene 57) preserve his competence and initiative.
personality_voice.difference: Several personality nuances are compressed or missing. The book Ron's wit is richer and more layered — his banter during the Horcrux discussions (e.g., 'Oh, lucky we've got such a large supply of basilisk fangs,' 'I was wondering what we were going to do with them') shows a quicker, drier intelligence than the film captures. His emotional generosity — the extended comforting of Hermione when she cries over Mad-Eye, the handkerchief cleaned with Tergeo, the squeeze — is absent. The film Ron also loses the book Ron's tendency to initiate practical planning when Harry is passive: the entire Potterwatch-finding subplot, the ongoing 'Three Horcruxes left, let's plan' leadership during Harry's Hallows obsession, and the ghoul-with-spattergroit plan are either absent or reduced. The film compresses but does not fundamentally distort his voice; it simply removes layers of it.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main personality is preserved with the correct emotional register, humor, and directness. The penalty is for compression of his wit, loss of his nurturing side (the comforting of Hermione over Mad-Eye), and some flattening of his role as emotional anchor when Harry is distracted. Not severe enough for the 14–17 range because the defining traits — loyalty, bluntness, insecurity-alongside-courage, humor — are all observable in the film corpus. Minor-to-moderate simplification, not distortion.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Ron is a co-protagonist with meaningful agency at nearly every key juncture of the Deathly Hallows arc. He proposes and executes the ghoul-with-spattergroit plan to protect his family (Scenes 168–176). He is one of three planners of the Ministry infiltration, with specific reconnaissance contributions (knowledge of Ministry worker uniforms, Magical Maintenance colors). He casts the saving Imperio on Bogrod at the Ministry. He finds Potterwatch, invests weeks trying to tune in, and discovers the Taboo jinx through independent intelligence-gathering. During Harry's Hallows obsession, Ron actively takes charge of Horcrux planning — 'taking charge' is the narrator's explicit observation (Scene 1509). He figures out that they need to go to the Chamber of Secrets to get basilisk fangs — this is entirely his idea (Scene 2114–2116). He opens the Chamber using Parseltongue he learned from Harry in his sleep. He destroys the locket Horcrux after returning. He saves Harry from drowning. He delivers the first 'He beat you!' challenge to Voldemort's manipulation of the crowd. He initiates key decisions at multiple points.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve several of Ron's most important acts of agency: casting Imperio on Bogrod (Film Scene 44), the Parseltongue entry into the Chamber (Film Scene 57), destroying the Horcrux cup (Film Scene 60), saving Harry from drowning and destroying the locket (Film Scene 25), the 'Liar!' defiance of Voldemort (Film Scene 64), the vote for going to Lovegood (Film Scene 28), identifying Dolohov from wanted posters (Film Scene 10), and the 'Look inside him, Harry' instruction in Film Scene 63 (urging Harry to use Legilimency to locate Voldemort and the snake). Notably, the Chamber of Secrets plan is still Ron's idea in the film (Film Scene 56: 'It's Ron's idea. And it's brilliant'). His role as the one who proposes the snake-killing plan in the final stages is preserved.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Significant agency is lost or absent. The ghoul-with-spattergroit plan is entirely absent from the theatrical film — this was one of Ron's most proactive and strategically sophisticated contributions. The Potterwatch discovery is absent (the Bill's warning scene establishing the Taboo is cut, and the radio-finding subplot is cut). Ron's weeks of sustained leadership during Harry's Hallows obsession ('Three Horcruxes left, let's go') is unfilmed. Ron's knowledge of Magical Maintenance uniforms from Mr. Weasley — a practical intelligence contribution that shapes the Ministry plan — is removed in the theatrical cut (Bill's warning scene is excluded). The film Ron is more reactive and less proactive in the planning sequences. His role as emotional and strategic anchor during Harry's passive phase is substantially reduced.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Ron retains a number of important acts of agency (Chamber plan, Parseltongue, Horcrux destruction, Voldemort defiance, Imperio at Ministry, Deluminator return). However, the ghoul plan — his single most proactive and creative act in the whole book — is gone. The Potterwatch initiative, the sustained leadership during Harry's Hallows drift, and the Taboo discovery via independent intelligence are all absent. These are not minor trimmings; they constitute Ron's 'leadership when Harry is failing' function, which is a defined narrative role. This warrants a penalty but not catastrophic reduction, since his key plot-turning actions remain.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Ron's motivations in the books are layered: love for his family and terror of their being harmed, loyalty to Harry and Hermione as chosen family, deep-seated insecurity about always being second (to Harry, to his brothers), and genuine commitment to defeating Voldemort rooted in values rather than just allegiance. His departure is explicitly motivated by a confluence of Horcrux amplification of real insecurities (he genuinely fears being unloved by his mother, by Hermione, fears being perpetually overshadowed by Harry) combined with physical exhaustion, hunger, and fear for his family. His return is motivated by hearing Hermione's voice — not just love, but the Deluminator as symbol of Dumbledore's faith in him, implying he was always meant to find his way back. His post-return behavior — the self-imposed penance, the takeover of Horcrux planning — is motivated by genuine guilt and desire to prove himself.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve Ron's core motivations adequately. His departure scene (Film Scene 24) includes the 'YOUR PARENTS ARE DEAD, YOU HAVE NO FAMILY' outburst — preserving the family-fear motivation — and his jealousy about Harry and Hermione ('I saw you two the other night'). His return is preserved with the Deluminator mechanism and the explicit statement 'I think Dumbledore knew I'd run out... He knew she'd lead me back' (Film Scene 27), preserving the faith-and-redemption motivation. His defiance of Voldemort ('Liar!', Film Scene 64) and willingness to die for the mission preserve the values-based commitment. The family fear motivation is reinforced in the departure scene with his mention of Ginny and Fred and George on the Potterwatch radio.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film compresses but does not fundamentally alter Ron's motivations. However, the Horcrux's role in amplifying real insecurities is somewhat clarified in the book (Ron explicitly says 'it made me think stuff — stuff I was thinking anyway, but it made everything worse,' Scene 1191). In the film, Ron says something similar but the distinction between Horcrux-amplified and genuinely-felt is slightly less precise. The fear-for-family motivation is less developed in the film because the Potterwatch sequences — where Ron listens obsessively for names of his loved ones — are absent. His internal conflict during the Horcrux destruction (the visions of being least loved, second best) is preserved in the film.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified in the film but remain recognizably correct. The core drivers — family love, loyalty, insecurity, redemptive guilt — are all present. The main compression is the absence of the Potterwatch radio obsession, which in the books gives his 'listening every night for names' a visceral daily texture the film lacks. Minor simplification, not alteration.

character_arc.book_baseline: Ron's arc in Deathly Hallows is a maturation arc: he begins as a loyal but sometimes passive follower who defers to Harry's lead, becomes the one who breaks under accumulated pressure (the departure), and returns to demonstrate that his loyalty and love are not passive but actively chosen. After returning, the arc continues: Ron takes on leadership when Harry obsesses over the Hallows, and by the end he is a full co-equal participant in the final push. The arc has a clear emotional shape: fall (departure), recognition (hearing Hermione's voice), return (the forest), redemption (destroying the locket, leading the Horcrux planning), and final vindication (Chamber of Secrets, final battle). A key turning point is Ron explicitly admitting he was wrong and earning back his place through action, not words.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves the arc's basic shape. The departure is shown (Film Scene 24). The return via Deluminator is preserved (Film Scenes 25–27). The Horcrux destruction is preserved (Film Scene 25). The Chamber of Secrets initiative is preserved (Film Scene 56). The final battle participation and the Voldemort-defiance ('Liar!') are preserved. The emotional beats of the reunion — Hermione punching him, his apology, her sustained coldness — are shown.
character_arc.difference: The arc's middle section — Ron's sustained post-return leadership during Harry's Hallows obsession — is almost entirely absent from the film. In the books, there is an extended period (weeks) where Ron becomes the one keeping the Horcrux mission alive while Harry is distracted. The film jumps relatively quickly from Ron's return to the Lovegood visit without showing this phase. The arc therefore lacks a key developmental beat: Ron proving himself not just through dramatic acts (saving Harry from the pool) but through sustained daily effort and moral constancy. The Potterwatch discovery — Ron's proactive intelligence work — is also absent, further thinning the post-return arc. The arc is present and recognizable but missing important steps of its middle phase.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Arc is compressed and missing important steps in the middle section. The major beats (departure, return, redemption through action, final vindication) are all present. The sustained leadership phase is absent. This warrants a penalty for incompleteness but not for distortion — the arc still reaches the right destination via the right emotional journey, just with some rungs of the ladder removed.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Ron's three defining relationships in this arc are: (1) with Harry — a friendship of equals where Ron can challenge, support, and even resent Harry without their bond breaking; (2) with Hermione — a slow-burn romantic tension that manifests in protectiveness, jealousy, banter, and tenderness; (3) with his family — particularly the terror of his family being harmed, the guilt over leaving them, and the deep Weasley family loyalty. The Ron-Harry relationship is notable for Ron being able to tell Harry hard truths ('For you? You think Mad-Eye died for you?'), and for Harry genuinely needing Ron as a strategic and emotional anchor. The Ron-Hermione relationship has a specific emotional texture: Ron is tender and protective (the handkerchief scene, the arm-around-shoulder after Mad-Eye's death), jealous and insecure (Krum's appearance at the wedding), and ultimately willing to declare his feelings in the middle of a war.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Ron-Harry friendship is mostly preserved in its mutual respect and honesty. Ron's ability to challenge Harry is shown ('For you?... This is a whole lot bigger than that,' Film Scene 4; the yard confrontation). The Ron-Hermione dynamic is preserved in its romantic tension — the jealousy when Mary Cattermole kisses Ron (Film Scene 18), the Deluminator speech about hearing Hermione's voice (Film Scene 26), Hermione's punching him on return (Film Scene 26), and the near-confession during the snake chase (Film Scene 68). The family dimension is present in his mention of Ginny, Fred, and George in the departure argument.
key_relationships.difference: The Ron-Hermione relationship loses significant texture: the extended scenes of Ron being tender and nurturing (the Mad-Eye handkerchief, comforting Hermione over Horcrux books, giving her a squeeze) are absent. The film Ron-Hermione dynamic skews heavily toward jealousy and banter, with the quieter protective warmth less visible. The Ron-Harry relationship loses the 'sustained leadership when Harry is passive' dimension (see arc notes above), which in the books is the most significant evolution of that friendship in this period. The family relationship is present emotionally but lacks grounding in the Potterwatch obsession scenes, which gave it daily texture in the books. The kiss at the moment of the Horcrux destruction — 'now or never' — is present in the film (Film Scene 62, implied by the screenplay noting Hermione's hair running like silk), but the books make it explicit and earned; the film is more ambiguous at this point in the theatrical cut.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The key relationships are recognizable and functionally intact, but the emotional texture of the Ron-Hermione relationship is simplified (less nurturing warmth, more jealousy-banter), and the Ron-Harry 'friend as anchor' dynamic during Harry's passive phase is substantially thinned. These are meaningful alterations to dynamic rather than just compression of screen time.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The books present Ron as one of the trilogy's most complex secondary protagonists. His complexity comes from several sources: (1) his ability to be both right (about Dumbledore not telling them enough) and wrong (about leaving) simultaneously; (2) his role as the most 'normal' person in the group, which gives him a practical wisdom others lack; (3) his specific contradictions — cowardly in one moment, monumentally brave in the next; selfishly angry, then immediately self-aware and remorseful; (4) his capacity for emotional intelligence that surprises even Hermione (the tact Ron shows when she cries); (5) his being funny without being reduced to comic relief — his humor is often strategically deployed to defuse tension; (6) his unique wizarding-world knowledge (Beedle the Bard, Magical Maintenance uniforms, Potterwatch) that proves practically essential; (7) the ghoul plan as an emblem of proactive love.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves Ron's contradictions reasonably well — he is brave and insecure, funny and serious, protective and sometimes cruel (the 'Your parents are dead' line). His practical knowledge contributes (identifying Dolohov, suggesting the Chamber plan, casting Imperio). His humor is genuinely present without reducing him to buffoon status. The Deluminator speech (Film Scene 26) is one of the film's most nuanced Ron moments, preserving his self-awareness and emotional honesty about having needed a way back.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Several significant nuances are lost in the film: (1) The ghoul plan — Ron's single most inventive and emotionally generous act in the book — is entirely absent, removing evidence of his proactive love for his family and his strategic mind; (2) The sustained Potterwatch-radio obsession, which shows Ron's daily emotional investment in his family, is absent; (3) Ron's nurturing behavior toward Hermione (multiple scenes of physical comfort and emotional support) is largely absent from the film, making his tenderness invisible and skewing his characterization toward jealousy; (4) Ron's leadership during Harry's Hallows obsession — explicitly noted in the books as a character beat — is unfilmed; (5) Ron's specific debate-entry moments (the Horcrux book discussion about Horcrux destruction, the Peverell deductions, the 'Goblins can Disapparate from Hogwarts' insight) are mostly absent or transferred to Hermione. These losses do change the audience's understanding of who Ron is: without them, he reads as a loyal secondary figure rather than a complex co-protagonist with independent intellectual and moral contributions.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The film Ron is recognizably complex — he is not reduced to a single trait — but meaningful nuance is lost: the nurturing side, the strategic proactive love, the sustained leadership, the intellectual contributions. The character is substantially complete in its emotional shape but missing material that made him rich. This falls in the 8–10 range: noticeable simplification with important nuances missing, but not a collapse to a single trait.

lost_or_transferred_material: Ghoul-with-spattergroit plan: Ron's proactive and inventive plan to protect his family by disguising the Weasley ghoul as himself with spattergroit — entirely absent from the theatrical film
Potterwatch discovery: Ron spending weeks tuning the radio, discovering the password 'Albus', and the trio listening together to Lupin/Lee/Kingsley — absent from the theatrical film
Taboo jinx discovery: In the theatrical cut, the Bill's-warning scene is excluded; Ron's intelligence about the Taboo (overheard at the Ministry) appears in a cut scene only
Ron's sustained leadership phase: The book's explicit narration that Ron 'took charge' of Horcrux planning while Harry obsessed over the Hallows is entirely unfilmed
Comforting Hermione over Mad-Eye's death: Ron putting his arm around Hermione, cleaning the handkerchief with Tergeo, giving her a squeeze — absent from the film
Ron's practical Magical Maintenance uniform knowledge (from Arthur Weasley): this key detail that shaped the Ministry plan is in a cut scene only
Ron identifying Gregorovitch connection to Quidditch (Gorgovitch of the Chudley Cannons): absent from the film
Ron's Horcrux discussion contributions (Horcrux destruction methods, soul mechanics questions, Peverell deductions): most transferred to or dominated by Hermione in the film
Ron's 'Now or never' first kiss with Hermione during the battle — present in the book as an explicit, earned romantic moment; ambiguous or absent in the theatrical cut at that moment
Ron's 'goblins can Disapparate from Hogwarts when we can't' insight: absent from film
Arthur Weasley Muggle radio tinkering scene: cut from theatrical film
score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score above 75 if a core book function/decision/act of agency is transferred or removed): applied — the ghoul plan and the Potterwatch/sustained-leadership phase represent core agency that is absent; total is kept at or below 75
key_observations: The film's Ron Weasley is a faithful rendering of the character's emotional core — loyal, brave, funny, insecure, capable of both cruelty and profound tenderness — but loses significant depth in three specific areas. First, his proactive agency is substantially reduced: the ghoul plan (his most creative and loving act in the book), the Potterwatch initiative, and his sustained leadership during Harry's Hallows obsession are all absent, making him more reactive than the books portray. Second, his nurturing emotional intelligence — the side of him that comforts Hermione, reads the room, and acts with unexpected tact — is largely invisible in the film, skewing his characterization toward jealousy and banter at the expense of warmth. Third, his post-return arc lacks the sustained middle section in which he proves himself through daily constancy rather than a single dramatic act. The film is not unfair to Ron — it preserves the departure and return, his key Horcrux-destroying moments, the Chamber of Secrets initiative, and his defiance of Voldemort — but the cumulative effect of the removed material is a Ron who reads as a loyal secondary figure rather than the complex, occasionally necessary co-protagonist the books establish. A score of 71 reflects a portrayal that is recognizable and emotionally truthful in its broad strokes, but missing enough of the specific material that made him rich and agentic that it cannot score in the high range.
